sourceReviews.supportingSummary: Independently read the actual raw MCP JSON_ARRAYAGG (Transact-SQL) receipt, including its availability note, syntax, null-clause and order-clause arguments, return value, and examples 1 through 4. The note explicitly says this aggregate is generally available for Azure SQL Database while separately in Preview for SQL Server 2025. Its local ORDER BY controls aggregate element order; examples demonstrate ordering by a value and by a separate column identifier. NULL ON NULL emits a JSON null element for SQL NULL, whereas ABSENT ON NULL omits that element and is the default. The standard text-returning call yields an nvarchar(max) JSON array. No RETURNING json, Managed Instance policy, SQL Server 2022 aggregate availability, or table-input arrival-order guarantee is inferred.

choiceReviews.rationale: Ordering within JSON_ARRAYAGG by the distinct Position values gives the row sequence 10, 20, 30. NULL ON NULL keeps the middle SQL NULL Label as a JSON null element instead of discarding its position. The documentation-derived output is exactly ["z",null,"a"]. Both clauses are needed for the stated contract; this conclusion does not rely on the VALUES constructor's textual row order or an outer SELECT ordering. A is the only offered combination meeting the required order and three-slot shape.

The local ascending Position order is suitable, but ABSENT ON NULL omits the middle null-valued element. B therefore has ["z","a"] as its documented result, losing the required null slot. Positive countercontext: this exact aggregate over the same rows is correct for an export that requires only nonnull labels in increasing Position order, with ["z","a"] as its expected array. The source explicitly supports null-element omission and aggregate-local ordering for that alternative contract.

NULL ON NULL retains the middle slot, but descending Position orders the rows 30, 20, 10 and gives ["a",null,"z"], not the requested ascending-position array. Positive countercontext: retain this exact expression when the same export must run from highest Position to lowest while preserving null gaps, explicitly requiring ["a",null,"z"]. The documented local order clause controls the row sequence independently of the null policy, supporting that reversed-order contract.

This combination reverses Position order and drops the SQL NULL Label. The documentation-derived array is ["a","z"], so it satisfies neither the required ascending label order nor the retained null position. Positive countercontext: the exact aggregate is appropriate for a compact, nonnull-only list in descending Position order, with ["a","z"] as the requested output from the same rows. Both the descending order and omission policy then serve the changed contract; neither is correct for the actual target array.
